difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (reading a past counterfactual "had been … would have made" as contrary to fact), applied directly to four short statements; under a minute for a prepared student.
stem:
‘If his latest movie had been a commercial success, the actor would have made enough money to sponsor his next movie.’

Based only on the above sentence, which one of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The actor will certainly sponsor his next movie.

options.label: B
options.text: His latest movie was a commercial success.

options.label: C
options.text: The actor made enough money from his latest movie.

options.label: D
options.text: His latest movie was not commercially successful.

solution.quick: "If … **had been** …, … **would have made** …" is the past counterfactual (third conditional): it imagines a past that did **not** happen. So the sentence tells us the latest movie was **not** a commercial success (and the actor did not make that money). Answer: **(D)**.

steps.title: Identify the sentence structure
steps.body:
The sentence has the form

*If* + **past perfect** ("had been a commercial success"), *subject* + **would have** + past participle ("would have made enough money").

This is the **third conditional**, which English uses only for *hypothetical situations in the past that are contrary to fact*.

steps.title: Extract what the form implies about reality
steps.body:
A third-conditional sentence carries two implied facts:

1. The *if*-condition did **not** happen: the latest movie was **not** a commercial success.
2. The imagined result did **not** happen (as a consequence of that success): the actor did **not** make enough money from it to sponsor his next movie.

Compare "If his latest movie *is* a success, the actor *will* make enough money", which is an open possibility and implies nothing about what actually happened.

steps.title: Check each statement against the sentence alone
steps.body:
- **(A)** "will certainly sponsor his next movie": the sentence says nothing about the future with certainty; it only describes an unrealised past possibility. Not supported.
- **(B)** "was a commercial success": contradicts implied fact 1. False.
- **(C)** "made enough money from his latest movie": contradicts implied fact 2. False.
- **(D)** "was not commercially successful": exactly implied fact 1. **True.**

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Based only on the given sentence, the one statement that must be true is **(D)**: his latest movie was not commercially successful.

solution.finalAnswer: **(D)** His latest movie was not commercially successful.
solution.teaching:
**Conditionals and what they say about reality.** English "if" sentences come in a few standard forms, and the verb forms tell you whether the condition is real, possible or imaginary:

| Type | Form | Example | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zero | if + present, present | If you heat ice, it melts. | general truth |
| First | if + present, will + verb | If it rains, we will stay in. | real, open possibility |
| Second | if + past, would + verb | If I were rich, I would travel. | imaginary present: I am not rich |
| Third | if + had + past participle, would have + past participle | If she had studied, she would have passed. | imaginary past: she did not study and did not pass |

The second and third conditionals are **counterfactual**: the speaker is talking about something that is *not* (or was *not*) the case. A GATE reasoning question that says "based only on the above sentence" is testing exactly this implied meaning.

Note the contrast with formal logic. A bare material implication "if P then Q" does not tell you whether P is true, and concluding "not Q" from "not P" would be the fallacy of denying the antecedent. Here, though, we do not *infer* "not P" from anything: the **grammar of the third conditional itself asserts** that P was false. That is why "the movie was not a success" follows, while anything about the actor's *future* sponsoring does not.

**In this question**, "had been a commercial success … would have made enough money" is a third conditional, so the latest movie was not a commercial success, which is option **(D)**. Options (B) and (C) state the opposite of what the counterfactual implies, and (A) makes an unsupported claim about the future.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: The sentence describes an unrealised past possibility; it says nothing certain about what the actor *will* do. If anything, it implies he did not earn the money that would have funded the next movie.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: The third conditional ("had been … would have") signals that the condition was contrary to fact, so the movie was **not** a commercial success. (B) states the opposite.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: "Would have made enough money" describes money he would have made in the imagined scenario; the counterfactual form implies he did **not** make it. (C) contradicts the sentence.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: The past counterfactual form implies its condition was false: his latest movie was **not** commercially successful.

solution.shortcut: Spot "had + past participle … would have + past participle": it is always contrary to past fact. Negate the if-clause and pick that option.
solution.commonTrap: Treating the sentence as a plain logical "if P then Q" and concluding nothing can be inferred about P (or picking (C) by reading the result clause as a fact). The verb form "had been … would have made" itself tells you the condition did not happen.
